intro: Freedom of Information (FOI) laws are a cornerstone of democratic governance. They give citizens, journalists, and civil society organisations the right to access government-held information and to hold public authorities accountable.

Yet, in practice, FOI laws often fail to deliver the transparency formally promised by legislation. Public administrations may respond fully, provide only partial information, refuse access, delay responses, or fail to respond at all.

TRANSACT studies this gap between formal transparency rights and everyday administrative practice. The project examines how FOI laws are implemented through concrete interactions between citizens and public officials, and how these interactions are shaped by request characteristics, bureaucratic discretion, and broader political, administrative, and socio-economic contexts.

The project combines implementation audits, observational studies using large-scale FOI platform data, and randomised field experiments to assess administrative compliance, identify patterns of transparency in practice, and explain the factors influencing bureaucratic responsiveness. Its comparative research spans multiple national and supranational settings, including Belgium, Romania, Switzerland, Armenia, South Africa, South Korea, Canada, and the European Union.
By explaining when and why FOI laws work in practice, TRANSACT aims to advance research on transparency governance, democratic accountability, and citizen–state relations.
